summary: This standards-track RFC defines an EDNS(0) Padding option so DNS clients and servers can pad requests and responses by a variable number of octets. Padding makes message sizes less revealing when DNS traffic is encrypted.

plainLanguage.summary: Even a sealed message shows how big it is, and size can give away what it contains. This option adds blank filler so messages of the same kind look the same size, but it only helps when the traffic is also encrypted.

questions: dns padding to hide message size
can i use dns padding without encryption
subtitle: A DNS option that lets clients and servers add filler bytes so encrypted messages reveal less through their size.

tldr.problem: Even when DNS messages are encrypted, their size is metadata that could be used to match them against well-known unencrypted messages.
tldr.mechanism: The EDNS(0) Padding option, option code 12, lets a client or server add a variable number of padding octets inside the OPT record, which hides the true size of the message.
tldr.outcome: Padding helps only on encrypted transport, so implementations MUST NOT use the option when the DNS transport is not encrypted.

facts.label: Occurrences
facts.value: At most once per OPT meta-RR

today: RFC 7830 is a Standards Track document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. IANA updated the registry record for option code 12 to reference this RFC with status Standard.

sections.title: Why Pad Encrypted DNS
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) (RFC 1035) was specified to carry messages in cleartext, which can expose a lot about an end user's Internet activity. The IETF has since worked on giving DNS transactions confidentiality, and encrypting the transport is one option.

RFC 7830 points out that even if both the query and the response were encrypted, metadata could still be used to correlate such messages with well-known unencrypted messages, which would spoil some of the confidentiality gained. One such property is message size. The RFC defines the EDNS(0) Padding option so clients and servers can artificially increase the size of a DNS message by a variable number of bytes, which hampers size-based correlation.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption hides what a message says, but not how big it is. Adding filler in the padding makes every message of a kind look about the same size, so an observer cannot use size to guess what it is.

sections.title: The Padding Option
sections.content:
EDNS(0) (RFC 6891) lets new options ride in the RDATA of the OPT meta-RR. The Padding option is made of an OPTION-CODE, an OPTION-LENGTH that is the size in octets of the padding, and then the padding octets themselves. The minimum number of padding octets is 0. The option MUST occur at most once per OPT meta-RR, and therefore at most once per message.

The padding octets SHOULD be set to 0x00. Other values MAY be used, for example when there is concern that the padded message could be compressed before encryption. Receivers MUST accept padding octets of any value.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is a small label that says "filler here" and how much of it there is, followed by the filler itself. The filler is usually just blank bytes.

sections.title: When to Pad
sections.content:
The RFC does not say how much to pad, because that depends on the situation. A padded message MUST NOT exceed the number of octets in the Requestor's Payload Size field, which is encoded in the RR Class field. The rules for responders are:

  • Responders MUST pad a response when the query included the Padding option, unless that would violate the maximum UDP payload size.
  • Responders MAY pad a response when the query showed EDNS(0) support but did not include the option.
  • Responders MUST NOT pad a response when the query did not indicate EDNS(0) support.
sections.plainLanguage: If your query asked for padding, you get a padded reply. If your query only showed that you can handle it, you might get one. If you cannot handle it, you never do. The message must still fit the size limit you allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Padding makes packets bigger, so it leads to more traffic. It gives a benefit only when DNS packets are not sent in cleartext, and it may make DNS amplification attacks easier. Therefore implementations MUST NOT use the option if the DNS transport is not encrypted.

Padding length might be changed by lower-level compression, so implementations and deployments SHOULD disable compression at the Transport Layer Security (TLS) level, as described in Section 3.3 of RFC 7525. The RFC also notes that the padding payload could be used as a covert channel, like many other fields in DNS. IANA has assigned Option Code 12 for Padding and updated its registry record to reference this RFC with status Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Filler only helps if the message is also encrypted. It makes the traffic heavier and could even help attackers flood a target, so it must not be used without encryption. Someone could also try to hide a secret message in the blank filler.
